# Parachute (`parachute`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/navigation.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Navigation, transport & exploration (`navigation`)
- Deps: helped by textile_fibres, hot_air_hydrogen_balloon
- Core idea: An open canopy presents a large area to the airflow. Drag increases with descent speed until it balances the weight of the person and equipment. For a given canopy a heavier load descends faster. Venting and the porosity of the fabric affect oscillations. Leonardo drew a linen pyramid on a rigid frame around 1485. In 2000 Adrian Nicholas descended under a reconstruction, then separated from the frame and landed under a modern parachute.
- Pitfalls:
  - Canopies too small; descent speed depends on total mass, air density, canopy area and drag; even a fully opened canopy can land hard
  - Jumping from too low a height for the canopy to open
  - Crediting the idea to Leonardo alone; a Sienese manuscript of the 1470s already shows a conical parachute
- History: europe: 1470s – conical parachute in a Sienese manuscript (British Library Add. MS 34113); c. 1485 Leonardo's pyramid design; c. 1615–16 Faust Vrančić's Homo volans; 1783 Lenormand's jump from a tower in Montpellier; 1797 Garnerin jumps from a balloon over Paris
- Read:
  - Fausto Veranzio, Machinae novae (Venice, c. 1615–16)
  - Lynn White Jr., The Invention of the Parachute, Technology and Culture 9, no. 3 (1968), 462–467
